result:
Not quite — training your own model with PPO isn't what gets your makerspace assistant to call tools better. That premise mixes up two different things.

Here's the real split: yes, big labs like Anthropic or OpenAI use reinforcement learning (PPO is one method) to train their models to be good at following instructions and using tools *in general*. That happens once, inside the lab, with huge GPU clusters and ML research teams, before the model ever ships. It's genuinely part of how "the best agents" get built — so the thing you read wasn't wrong.

But you're not building a model, you're building on top of one. For your assistant, "calling tools better" is a design and prompting problem, not a training problem. Concretely: if your `book_equipment` tool is described as `book_equipment(info)` with no detail, the model will guess wildly at what `info` should contain. Rename it to `book_equipment(equipment_name: str, date: str, time: str)` with a one-line description of each, and the model calls it correctly almost every time — zero math, zero GPUs, just a better tool definition and some testing.

That's squarely your job over the next five weeks: writing tool descriptions, shaping what the model sees, deciding when to retry or stop. Training a model from scratch needs compute and data you don't have and isn't what your sponsor is paying for.

Does that distinction make sense — where RL training lives (inside the lab, once) versus where your work lives (on top of the model, every time you write a tool)?
